routes.description: Establish consciousness as the sole fundamental ontology and explain objective order, individual perspectives, causality, and nonspatiotemporal structure as configurations of universal subjectivity.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if a consciousness-only ontology avoids emergence while accounting for empirical regularity, external reality, differentiated subjects, causal efficacy, and structured relations without fundamental spacetime.

motionBridge.description: Show that consciousness is a more parsimonious and explanatorily complete ontological foundation than non-conscious matter or neutral primitives.

centralBridges.description: Explain how an observer-independent and scientifically ordered world can consist of external mental states represented through perception.
Explain individual selves and experiences as differentiated modes or excitations of one universal subjectivity.
Ground causal regularity in intrinsic properties and interactions within a single mental ontology.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Connect physics, neuroscience, altered experience, and consciousness theory to predictions or implications consistent with idealism.
Account for fundamental structure through semantic or cognitive relations that do not require spatial or temporal extension.

routes.description: Deny that failures of materialist emergence establish idealism by developing a neutral representational alternative and testing whether idealism explains structure, causality, and subjecthood.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if neutral representational processes avoid the hard problem while consciousness-first language fails to add necessary explanatory content concerning ordered structure, causal agents, or experience.

motionBridge.description: Show that avoiding matter-to-consciousness emergence does not require treating consciousness as the ontological foundation of reality.

centralBridges.description: Locate phenomenal character in representations without positing either separately existing physical objects or universal consciousness as substance.
Require an account of how representations, organism boundaries, and predictable order arise rather than merely labeling their inaccessible substrate mental.
Determine where causal efficacy resides when the ordinary personal self is constructed, unstable, or absent.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish correlations or mappings involving integrated information from an explanation of why subjective experience exists.
Test whether theories framed through brains, fields, vibrations, or processes can accommodate experience without ordinary space and time.

sections.title: Ontological foundation and empirical warrant
sections.rationale: The motion turns first on whether consciousness is the most economical fundamental given and whether available empirical considerations distinguish that proposal from a neutral alternative.

sections.title: External reality and explanatory structure
sections.rationale: A consciousness-first ontology must preserve an observer-independent ordered world and specify how perception, organisms, and regularities arise within its single category.

sections.title: Representation, self-models, and experience
sections.rationale: The distribution of phenomenal character across representations and the status of the personal self determine whether neutral representation suffices or still presupposes consciousness.

sections.title: Integrated information and explanatory scope
sections.rationale: Integrated information bears on the persistence and causal role of experience, but its relevance depends on whether it supplies operational prediction, metaphysical explanation, or limited ontological implications.

sections.title: Subjecthood and the source of causality
sections.rationale: The ontology must identify the bearer and source of causal efficacy when personal selves are modeled as constructed and dream contents may arise without an experienced agent.

sections.title: Structure without fundamental spacetime
sections.rationale: The account of fundamental reality must preserve differentiation and meaningful structure even when ordinary spatial and temporal organization is absent or nonfundamental.
